glossary.Leukaemia: Cancer of white blood cells that starts in the bone marrow.
glossary.White blood cells: Immune cells in the blood: neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils and basophils.
glossary.Malignant: Cancerous: growing uncontrollably and able to invade.
glossary.Translocation: Swapping of pieces between two chromosomes.
glossary.Radiation exposure: Contact with ionising radiation, which damages DNA.
glossary.Chemotherapy: Drugs that kill rapidly dividing cancer cells.
glossary.Splenomegaly: An enlarged spleen; often massive in CML.
glossary.Systolic murmur: A heart sound heard between S1 and S2; a soft flow murmur can come from anaemia.
glossary.Marrow infiltration: Cancer cells filling the bone marrow and pushing out normal cells.
glossary.Night sweats: Drenching sweats at night, a sign of systemic disease.
glossary.Cytopenias: Low counts of one or more blood cell types.
glossary.Prognostic factor: A feature that predicts how well or badly the disease will go.
glossary.Testicular involvement: Leukaemia cells in the testis, a relapse site in boys with ALL.
glossary.Lymph node biopsy: Removing a lymph node or part of one to examine under the microscope.
glossary.FBC: Full blood count: haemoglobin, white cells and platelets.
glossary.Blood film: A drop of blood smeared on a slide and stained to look at cell shapes.
glossary.Basophils: Rare white cells with dark granules that release histamine; raised in CML.
glossary.Eosinophils: White cells involved in allergy and parasite defence; raised in CML.
glossary.Myeloid: The marrow cell line that makes neutrophils, monocytes, red cells and platelets.
glossary.Azurophilic granules: Purple-staining granules in myeloid cells containing enzymes such as myeloperoxidase.
glossary.Myeloperoxidase: An enzyme in neutrophil and myeloblast granules; positive staining marks myeloid cells.
glossary.Cytoplasm: The inside of a cell outside the nucleus.
glossary.Fusion protein: A protein made from two genes joined by a translocation.
glossary.Fusion gene: A hybrid gene formed when pieces of two genes are joined.
glossary.Tyrosine kinase inhibitor: A drug that blocks a growth-signalling enzyme; imatinib is one.
glossary.Supportive care: Treatment of symptoms and complications, such as transfusions and antibiotics.
glossary.Transfusion: Giving donated blood products into a vein.
glossary.Neutropenia: A low neutrophil count, leaving the patient open to severe infection.
glossary.Clonal: All descended from one original abnormal cell.
glossary.Haematopoietic stem cell: A marrow stem cell that can make every type of blood cell.
glossary.Progenitor cell: An early cell committed to becoming a particular blood cell line.
glossary.Erythroid: Relating to the red cell line.
glossary.Megakaryocytic: Relating to megakaryocytes, the large marrow cells that make platelets.
glossary.Precursors: Immature cells that develop into mature blood cells.
glossary.Constitutively active: Switched on all the time, without the normal signal.
glossary.PML: A gene on chromosome 15 fused to RARA in acute promyelocytic leukaemia.
glossary.RARA: Retinoic acid receptor alpha gene on chromosome 17, needed for myeloid cells to mature.
glossary.Differentiation: The process of an immature cell maturing into its final form.
glossary.Lymphocytes: White cells of the adaptive immune system (B and T cells).
